articles.title: The fiscal cost of cash-transfer schemes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Business Standard reported on May 13, 2026 that “Cash-transfer promises have moved from the margins of Indian election manifestos to the centre of political competition, with parties across States promising monthly or one-time payments.” Quoting a PRS Legislative Research report, it further said, “12 States are expected to spend nearly ₹1.68 trillion on unconditional cash-transfer schemes for women in 2025-26, … the outgo is roughly equivalent to 0.5 per cent of India’s GDP, compared with less than 0.2 per cent two years ago.”

The RBI report ‘State Finance: Study of State Budgets 2025-26’ reported that the total subsidy outlay increased from ₹1.87 trillion in 2018-19 to ₹4.26 trillion in 2025-26. States often implement promises from their election manifestos soon after forming the government and just before the next election, without any serious assessment of needs or financial commitments.

Conception and funding of an infrastructure project are guided by a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that specifies objectives, alternatives considered, financial and economic analysis, risk mitigation, baseline data, and success criteria. A social policy, by contrast, is often the outcome of an electoral promise or based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any comparable ex ante appraisal. Social policies affect human capabilities more directly than infrastructure projects.

The scarcity of public resources and their alternative uses make ex ante appraisal of social sector schemes essential. Moreover, social policies are vulnerable to electoral clientelism, and should therefore adhere to the same principles of public expenditure as infrastructure projects — evidence, accountability, equity, efficiency and fiscal responsibility as infrastructure. The claim that the benefits of social policies are not quantifiable should not stop ex ante appraisal, as methodologies exist to overcome this barrier.

An ex ante appraisal of a social project leaves an audit trail: the legislature, auditors, the media, and citizens can ask whether the project delivered what it promised. Many social schemes are implemented without the assessment of needs, identification of potential beneficiaries, or adequate funding, and a bureaucratic, top-down, target-chasing approach often replaces a democratic, bottom-up planning and implementation process.
This article explores the fiscal and economic fallout of cash transfers and universal subsidies.

If politics decides the desired social ends of such schemes, public finance and administration should decide the programme’s funding priority, the quantum of funding and the implementation process required to achieve those ends.

Prioritising expenditure is the first step in checking the desirability of public expenditure. For example, the Government of Tamil Nadu allocated nearly ₹1,000 crore in 2026-27 to provide scholarships for girls and boys from Government schools to continue higher education. A recent report in a Tamil Magazine ( Ananda Vikatan , November 18, 2026), based on replies it received to RTI applications, found 7,198 vacancies in permanent teaching positions in Government Arts and Science Colleges. If we include teacher vacancies in professional colleges and universities, the number should be nearly 9,000. Filling these vacancies, delayed for over a decade, would cost ₹1,080 crore per annum, rising every year thereafter. With a huge revenue deficit and fiscal deficit, the State budget lacks the revenue cushion to spend an additional ₹1,080 crore per annum. Prioritising is a normative decision: filling vacancies ensures students learn from regular teachers, whereas funding scholarships alone sends them to colleges without regular teachers.

Deciding the quantum of funding and the process of execution requires ex ante evaluation. This should be explicitly oriented toward designing programmes that maximise impact for a given cost, using behavioural models and micro-simulations to predict the effects of hypothetical programmes before implementation.

For instance, a universal subsidy scheme is a trade-off between inclusion and exclusion errors. If it is truly universal, the scheme commits the error of including the undeserving and thus reduces the per-capita benefit to people in need. In a target-oriented scheme, it commits the error of excluding the deserving, but it increases the per-capita benefit to people in need. The choice between the two requires ex ante appraisal of such schemes.

Cash transfers and subsidies are perpetual in nature as they are politically hard to reverse. Therefore, the continuous commitment of scarce financial resources demands not only prior evaluation but also real-time monitoring and evaluation to redesign and right-size schemes.

In practice, fiscal constraints are addressed through post-hoc adjustments, usually by increasing borrowing or cutting even essential public expenditure. Fiscal constraints should, however, prompt more disciplined choices.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The tariffs are not final yet, with the U.S. government opening a window for written comments and requests to testify by January 5, 2027. Public hearings will begin on January 25, 2027, following which the final action will be communicated.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.
“Strong bank and non-bank credit growth continues to support the domestic economy. Further, sustained double-digit export growth broadened the base of economic expansion,” they added.
Equity markets remained buoyant amid robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio investment inflows, while net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Duty-free raw sugar imports up to 10 lakh tonnes allowed till March 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will be permitted until the end of March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) on Wednesday.

A notification issued on August 20 had allowed duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) scheme until December 31, 2026. Separately, the DGFT has allowed sugar mills time until September 30, 2027, to process the imported raw sugar and sell it in the domestic market.

The Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association Director General Deepak Ballani told The Hindu that price parity had prevailed over the past, making it viable for Indian importers to source raw sugar from international markets, primarily Brazil. Some imports have already begun.

The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season. It will also keep the prices stable, he said.

articles.title: Chinese Military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: China is staging a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in the province facing Taiwan, testing a new method to land troops ashore by linking civilian vessels ‌into a makeshift floating bridge, satellite images and a research report showed.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as ​its own territory, despite Taipei's rejection of Beijing's sovereignty claims, and has never renounced the use of force to ⁠bring it under Chinese control.

The exercise, in Dacheng Bay in China's southeastern province of Fujian, was first spotted on November 1, according to satellite images and a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters.

"The People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support ‌to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario," said Jason Wang, the company's chief operating officer.
"Using civilian ships to enable bridging of heavy equipment and materiel from deeper waters creates additional locations they can use ‌along the Taiwan coastline."

A senior security official briefed on the drill in Dacheng Bay, just 280 km (175 miles) from ‌Taiwan's ⁠main island, confirmed it was still in progress on Friday, but made no direct link to local elections ⁠set for the next day.

Analysis of the images from November 1 to 16 showed the vessels manoeuvred around the bay, forming and dismantling a floating bridge about 800 m (2,600 ft) long, in activity also seen in images from commercial providers Vantor and Planet Labs.

Eight civilian vessels participated, made up ​of four barges, two semi-submersible and two powered, along with ‌four landing craft, as well as smaller support vessels and Chinese navy ships nearby, ingeniSPACE's analysis and tracking data showed.

No purpose-built bridging equipment was observed, suggesting China's military may be honing its use of existing civilian maritime resources to improvise landing infrastructure in a combat scenario, ingeniSPACE said.
The senior security official confirmed the report details.

The drill was designed to "practise the swift seizure ‌of small islands" and was "very targeted" at contingencies along the first island chain, the arc of islands stretching from ​Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines, the official said.

It appeared to be part of this year's "All-Military Strategic Exercise" by the Chinese military, and was routine but held later than in previous years, added the official, ⁠who sought anonymity, as the matter is a sensitive one.

articles.title: Saudi strike kills 11 in Yemen, reports Houthi media
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A Saudi strike killed 11 people on Friday (November 27, 2026) in Yemen, Houthi media said, as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it shot down a drone targeting Riyadh.
The latest incidents came a day after a deadly Houthi attack on a Saudi oil refinery, and add to a growing tally of violence since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.
The coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Iran-allied Houthis, has been regularly bombing areas under their control.
Ukraine says it struck two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region
In response, Houthi forces have been targeting the oil-rich kingdom almost daily, hitting energy facilities, airports and the financial district of the capital, Riyadh.

Saudi warplanes carried out a raid on a residential building in the city of Al-Turba in Taiz governorate on Friday, killing "11 citizens, most of them children", the Houthis' Saba news agency said, citing a local source.
The agency also reported strikes targeting fuel tanks in the Saada region, the movement's birthplace and stronghold.

On Thursday (November 26, 2026), the Houthis targeted the Jazan refinery in southern Saudi Arabia, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several other people, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The attack also triggered a fire that led to the shutdown of the facility, SPA said.
Yemen plunged back into war in July, after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the West Asia war.

Hostilities intensified in September when the Houthis, who already controlled Yemen's most densely populated areas, seized the western coastline overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait on the Red Sea.
The Houthis are now advancing toward Aden, a major southern city where the government has taken refuge after being driven out of the capital Sanaa in 2015.

articles.title: NATO jets scrambled after drone enters Latvian airspace
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: NATO fighter jets and an interceptor drone were scrambled overnight in Latvia after a drone briefly entered the country's airspace near its border with Russia, the Army said Friday (November 27, 2026).
Since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.
This year, two drones were shot down over Latvia by NATO fighter jets, which protect the skies of Baltic states.
An Army statement said that during the night from Thursday to Friday a drone "briefly flew over Latvian territory" near the border with Russia.

"Fighter jets from NATO's air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed," it said, without specifying the origin of the drone.

articles.title: Hackers breach U.S. Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with ‌the matter told Reuters , in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, ​personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so ⁠during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In ‌a statement to Reuters , the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the ‌Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities."

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve ‌as ⁠a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, ⁠Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions ​System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than ‌200 U.S. Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the U.S. military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.
"A breach here ‌is a big deal," one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's ​cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.

The discovery of the hack led to a ⁠range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

Updates to applications already running on Cloud One ‌were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.

One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers ‌did so in this case.

articles.title: Hyderabad’s air pollution puts focus on hospitals; doctors call for city-level health database
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: With Hyderabad recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 300 on Deepavali and many other days recording poor air quality earlier this year, doctors and public health experts have called for a coordinated effort by hospitals to track the health effects of pollution and build a city-level database that can help shape public policy.

The issue came into focus during a panel discussion on ‘Impact of Mobility on Air Quality and Public Health’ at Cyberabad Moves, where doctors said that the effects of polluted air went beyond respiratory illnesses and were also linked to cardiovascular problems and strokes. They stressed that the health consequences of daily exposure to pollution, particularly during commutes, needed to be documented through local medical data.

Pawan Mukulutla of WRI India, who moderated the discussion, pointed out that congestion was only the most visible consequence of the way people travelled. The less visible costs included exposure to polluted air, unsafe roads and the lack of pedestrian infrastructure. He cited Hyderabad’s AQI crossing 300 on Deepavali and said particulate matter levels, including PM2.5 and PM10, had been several times above prescribed thresholds.

Dr. Sudheer Vinnamala, Regional Medical Director of KIMS, said hospitals could work together to create a Hyderabad-level health database by sharing anonymised information on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions with public health authorities.

“What you can’t measure, you can’t manage,” he said, arguing that such a database could help identify vulnerable groups and establish a clearer picture of the relationship between air quality and health outcomes.

He said doctors could also use daily AQI information to alert patients with asthma and other respiratory conditions when pollution levels deteriorated, allowing them to take precautions and avoid unnecessary exposure. Hospitals could play a role in reducing pollution and traffic by encouraging carpooling, staggering appointments and arranging last-mile transport links from Metro stations.

Dr Vishwanath Gella, a pulmonologist at AIG Hospitals, said pollution affected people with and without pre-existing health conditions. He said doctors were seeing patients with asthma, respiratory infections and other lung-related complaints, with an increase in cases during periods of poor air quality, particularly around Deepavali and in winter.

Dr Shailaja Tetali of the Public Health Foundation of India said research into school travel patterns showed that around 80 per cent of children lived within two to three kilometres of their schools. A majority travelled by public transport, walked or cycled.

While walking and cycling offered physical activity, children using these modes were also exposed to roadside pollution and faced road safety risks. She said improving infrastructure around schools could address several of these concerns, as interventions within a three-kilometre radius could cover a large proportion of children’s daily journeys.

She called for authorities to act on existing evidence instead of repeatedly commissioning studies, suggesting that interventions could first be tested in smaller areas and then replicated across the city.

Orthopaedic surgeon Dr Gurava Reddy of KIMS-Sunshine Hospitals said poorly designed roads and junctions contributed to crashes, pointing to inadequate visibility, obstructed sightlines and sudden turning movements as factors that made roads dangerous.
He said several improvements could be made through better road engineering without requiring large investments, provided authorities were willing to address design flaws.

articles.title: Robotic technology can improve precision and recovery in knee replacement, say experts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Hindu , in association with Kauvery Hospital, conducted a webinar on Friday titled ‘The Role of Robotics in Knee Replacement’. Orthopaedic specialists discussed the use of robotic-assisted technology in total knee replacement (TKR), its benefits, post-operative recovery, costs and the role of surgeons in performing the procedure.

The experts were Mukunth K., senior consultant, orthopaedic surgeon, joint replacement and sports injuries, Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet; P.R. Ramasamy, head of the department of orthopaedics and pelviacetabular and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Tiruchi; and Manivannan, consultant, orthopaedics, arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Salem.

Dr. Mukunth explained how robotic-assisted technology helps surgeons plan knee replacement procedures through bone mapping, precise measurements and real-time guidance. articles.title: COP31: India welcomes $50 million climate fund pledge, says adaptation needs far greater
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India has welcomed a $50 million pledge to the Adaptation Fund at the UN climate change conference COP31 , but said the contribution was inadequate given the scale of adaptation needs in developing countries and stressed that financial pledges must translate into timely and accessible resources.

In a written interview with PTI , Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said the removal of the $120 billion adaptation finance figure from the proposed cover text, and the failure to reach an overarching agreement at COP31, were disappointing.

“The absence of an agreed formulation on the $120 billion adaptation finance figure in the final outcome is disappointing. It reflects the continuing difficulties in securing predictable financial commitments and agreement on how progress towards the existing goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 should be measured and monitored,” he said.

Mr. Yadav, however, noted that the absence of a cover decision did not extinguish developed countries’ commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement.

He said adaptation was not a secondary consideration but an immediate developmental necessity for millions of vulnerable people. India had consistently maintained that adaptation finance must be adequate, predictable, primarily public and substantially grant-based, he added.

“Developing countries should not be compelled to incur additional debt to protect vulnerable communities from climate impacts. At COP31, India worked closely with Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) and G77 (largest bloc of 134 developing nations plus China) partners to seek stronger outcomes on adaptation finance and implementation support,” Yadav said.

He said India would continue to push for enhanced financial support, transparency in delivery and implementation of existing commitments, particularly for the poorest and most climate-vulnerable countries.

Mr. Yadav said that the failure to reach consensus on the proposed overarching agreement, the Antalya Pact, should not overshadow progress made on other issues and that the nation continues to deliver substantial climate action through its domestic efforts and resources.

“India engaged constructively throughout the Conference, working closely with BASIC, Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and G77 to secure a balanced and equitable outcome. We regret that consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact could not be reached. However, this should not overshadow the substantive progress achieved on several important issues,” he said.

On procedural decisions at COP31, Mr. Yadav said the Climate Finance Work Programme decision had established a process for further discussions, while the outcome on the Just Transition Work Programme was more substantive.

The Climate Finance Work Programme decision provides for discussions ahead of COP32 and COP33, including submissions by parties, workshops, virtual dialogues and a high-level ministerial roundtable in 2027.
“While agreement on its substantive scope remains outstanding, the decision provides an opportunity to advance discussions on developed countries’ obligations,” he said.

articles.title: Bombay High Court puts road project on hold till State files report on mangrove loss, compensatory measures
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Bombay High Court has withheld permission for a road project in Mumbai until the State government submits a detailed report on measures taken to compensate for the loss of mangroves. The court also stated that ‘afforestation’ efforts must be completed before seeking clearances and that the process should not be treated as a mere formality.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh C. Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna made these remarks while hearing a plea by the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) seeking permission to divert 0.2869 hectares of mangrove land in the Bandra-Kurla Complex area to construct an Automated Rapid Transit System covering 8.85 km.

A 2018 High Court ruling mandated court approval for developments affecting wetlands. Though the project will not require clearing mangroves, it impacts six trees, necessitating the planting of 100 trees as compensation.

Advocate Saket Mone, representing the MMRDA, argued that the Automated Rapid Transit System fulfills key connectivity needs. He added that tree planting falls under the jurisdiction of the Forest Department. In response, the Bench questioned why officials had not initiated remedial action when conceptualising the project.

Advocate General of Maharashtra Milind Sathe attributed the planting delays to a shortage of saline land, noting that saplings must be planted before the monsoon to ensure survival. However, the Bench pointed out a gap between regulators’ filings and ground reality, questioning how authorities could grant permission when rules mandate 30% tree cover.

The Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed. Stating that it does not oppose the project but will not proceed without full compliance, the Court posted the matter to November 30.
Mr. Mone was briefed by advocate Fatema Ansari, while Mr. Sathe was briefed by Government Pleader Onkar Chandurkar.

articles.title: Pressure tactics: On the new U.S. tariffs on India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014.

Yet, even a basic assessment of India’s import dependence and the fact that manufacturing’s share in GDP is lower now than a decade ago shows that India is far from having excess manufacturing capacity in any sector. Further, higher tariffs are unlikely to reduce America’s imports of the goods from India that it does depend on. The USTR mentioned generic pharmaceuticals, telecommunication equipment, and renewable energy goods. The first two are items that India has developed expertise in, which is distinct from strategic excess capacity. A relatively small tariff disadvantage will not substantially erode the attractiveness of these Indian products. Renewable energy imports from India have swelled because the U.S. is reducing its purchases from China. Hanging over all of this are the 100% tariffs related to the purchase of Russian oil, which have only temporarily been paused. India has so far held off on signing a deal, and must go ahead with one only if it is convinced that the benefits at least equal the costs.

articles.title: Indefensible defiance: On Tamil Nadu and Court’s Thirupparankundram order
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: By defying the Supreme Court’s one-time direction to also light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at a stone pillar , claimed by Hindu groups to be a Deepathoon, atop the Thirupparankundram hills, the Tamil Nadu government has disregarded a constitutional body’s authority. Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights.

Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Beyond generosity: on India-Nepal ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The state visit of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah to Delhi, eight months after he was voted to power as leader of the ‘GenZ’ movement that ousted the previous government, was anticipated as a chance to reset the turbulent India-Nepal relationship. Bringing Mr. Shah to India for a state visit, his first, was particularly important, given the Modi government’s tense ties with his predecessor K.P. Sharma Oli’s government; Mr. Oli was not invited to Delhi more than a year into his term and travelled to Beijing instead. Initially, Mr. Shah had also given New Delhi some worrying moments, with comments about boundary disputes, and a refusal to confirm a meeting with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, which led to the cancellation of his visit in May. Subsequently, some of the realities of governance, particularly after the massive flash flood in August , have warmed Delhi-Kathmandu relations. Following talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr. Shah thanked India for its immediate and unstinting support in the flood relief and rescue operations. Mr. Modi’s praise for Mr. Shah indicated the forging of a personal rapport on which to build the road map for ties. India announced a Development Cooperation Package — a generous ₹15,000 crore (about $1.6 billion) — for reconstruction and long-term development in Nepal. Another announcement, to offer Nepal access to Indian ports in Gujarat and Odisha, will go a long way in helping land-locked Nepal, particularly given the bilateral bad blood over the 2015 trade blockade. The inauguration of bridges, roads, trains, energy and fuel lines, an Integrated Check post (ICP) and an agreement to set up an IIT (its third offshore campus) are all signs of concrete plans to improve relations, as outlined in the joint statement titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal: Re-imagining the Partnership”.

Despite some of the heated rhetoric over ties, both sides appeared to have decided to deal with areas of differences in a less public manner. Mr. Shah’s persistent comments on the boundary dispute, and long-pending request for overflight access for two debt-ridden airports, were not dealt with directly, but in a broad reference about resolving “all outstanding matters” through dialogue. While the joint statement also said they would review all bilateral treaties, New Delhi’s contention that the “Eminent Persons Group” (EPG) report that suggested important changes to the 1950 Friendship treaty, is now “not relevant”, will ruffle feathers in Kathmandu which has been keen to update the treaty. The government must remember that along with the grand gestures, it is important to keep a close eye on Nepal’s grievances as well. If disregarded, these can trip up the broader progress and conception of the bilateral relationship, as spelt out by both leaders.

articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Sthanika Bhattars make contradictory statements on the lighting of deepam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Sthanika Bhattars of the Subramaniya Swamy Temple at Thirupparankundram gave some tense moments to the Madurai district administration by making contradictory statements on their “consent” for lighting the ceremonial lamp at the traditional spot — Deepa Mandapam — on Karthigai Deepam day.

The administration had submitted at the Supreme Court that despite its readiness to light the lamp at the deepathoon , it could not comply with the court directive as the temple’s Board of Trustees insisted on lighting the lamp only at the Deepa Mandapam, following age-old practices, customs and rituals, and agama rules.

A statement made on November 24 by the temple’s Executive Officer, G. Selvi, had said the reasoning for lighting the lamp at the Deepa Mandapam was backed by the Bhattars. However, the next day, a letter purportedly written by the Bhattars, stating that they had not given any letter of consent on lighting the lamp on November 24, went viral on social media. They said they had given consent for lighting the lamp at the usual spot near Uchipillaiyar Temple “last year” (2025). The recent statement by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department referring to their consent, made “without consulting” them, had caused mental agony, they said.

Meanwhile, there was commotion outside the house of Swaminatha Bhattar late in the evening on Wednesday, as functionaries of the BJP and Hindu outfits arrived at the priest’s house. Temple officials too were present at the house. The BJP functionaries said the Bhattars were being “forced” to give a new letter of consent to help the officials substantiate their stand before the Supreme Court. The demonstrators were detained by the police.

An official of the Department said the Bhattars gave the new letter on Wednesday to the Board of Trustees. “The lighting of Karthigai Deepam has been done at the Uchipillaiyar Temple since 1996 with the cooperation of the temple authorities,” said the letter, signed by four Bhattars. However, they underlined that they were only replying to a letter written by the temple administration, seeking their opinion on this issue.

They reasoned that the Utchipillaiyar Temple, the Rajagopuram, and the venue for burning chokkapanai near the 16-Pillar Mandapam lie on a straight line, and the Utchipillaiyar Temple was located right above the sanctum sanctorum. They also confirmed that they had given the same opinion “in writing” on November 7, 2013 and December 4, 2025. “The deepam is lit at the deepamandapam after getting oral or written opinion from us every year. This is in line with the agama rules and age-old Saiva customs,” they clarified.

articles.title: Karnataka’s Escoms plan to pass profits to consumers via lower power bills from April 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: In a relief for electricity consumers amid rising household expenses, electricity supply companies (Escoms) across Karnataka are likely to pass on their profits to consumers in the form of a refund of around 16 paise per unit from April 2027.

Sources in the Energy Department said on Thursday that most Escoms, including Bangalore Electricity Supply Company (Bescom), Gulbarga Electricity Supply Company (Gescom), Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Corporation (CESC), and Mangalore Electricity Supply Company (Mescom), have recorded profits for the financial year 2025-26. However, Hubli Electricity Supply Company (Hescom) is an exception.

A senior Energy Department official said the improved financial performance would enable Escoms to return the gains to consumers. Bescom alone reported a profit of ₹293.62 crore during 2025-26, while the profit figures of other Escoms are yet to be officially announced.

Every year, Escoms are required to submit their tariff status and profit-and-loss statements, known as truing-up petitions, to the Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (KERC) as part of their annual performance review. The companies are scheduled to submit their petitions on November 30.
Once the proposals receive KERC’s approval, the refund will be adjusted against electricity bills for consumption from April 2027.

While the average refund is expected to be around 16 paise per unit, consumers in some Escom jurisdictions could receive a higher benefit. Bescom sources said the company was seeking a refund of 35 paise per unit, although the proposal is yet to be finalised. The approved amount is expected to be announced on the Bescom website in December 2026.

Officials attributed the improved financial performance to a reduction in power distribution losses from 11% to around 9.13%. Escoms also reduced power procurement costs by utilising more electricity generated through hydropower instead of relying on relatively expensive thermal power.

articles.title: Workers of BJP, JD(S) stage protest opposing Operation Gaja at Kadabagere in Chikkamagaluru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Workers of the BJP and the JD(S) from Khandya hobli in Chikkamagaluru taluk jointly staged a protest at Kadabagere village on Thursday against Operation Gaja, the drive to push wild elephants from parts of Hassan district towards the Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary.

The workers took out a protest march in the village and raised slogans against the State government and the Congress MLAs, alleging that they had failed to represent the farmers affected by the government’s decision. They described the operation, which seeks to drive the elephants to the Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary, most of which lies in Chikkamagaluru district, as an unscientific move.

Former Minister D.N. Jeevaraj said the Forest Department should take responsibility for the crisis. “The plantations we have cultivated have become more comfortable habitats for elephants than the actual forest. The forest consists mostly of trees like acacia, which contribute little to its biodiversity. Hence, elephants find our plantations more suitable,” he said.

He also criticised the announcement by the Congress MLAs that they would resign, saying the legislators were only staging a drama instead of pressing the State government to protect the people of Chikkamagaluru from the elephant menace.

articles.title: Four-member gang targeting cab, bike taxi drivers arrested in Bengaluru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Whitefield police have busted an extortion racket and arrested four men who allegedly targeted cab and bike taxi drivers at night, assaulted them, and extorted money. The gang is suspected of having committed over two dozen such robberies in the past three months to fund their drug addiction and other vices.
The accused have been identified as Manoj, Preetham Prakash, Syed Shafi, and Akhilesh, residents of Gandhipura and Vijayanagar in Whitefield.

The arrests followed a complaint by Mohammed Nisar, a bike rider, who was allegedly intercepted and assaulted by the accused on an isolated stretch near Nallurhalli Metro station. The accused, who arrived in a car, allegedly assaulted him and forced him to transfer money online from his mobile phone before fleeing.
Following the complaint, a team of Whitefield police, led by DCP Haribabu, launched an operation to track down the gang.

The police traced the rental aggregator through which the accused had hired the car and followed the vehicle for around 2 km to 3 km. As the accused allegedly drove at high speed to evade the police, the investigators sought the rental company’s assistance in remotely switching off the car’s engine.

When the vehicle came to a halt, the accused stepped out to check the engine. Police personnel surrounded the car and arrested three of them on the spot. The fourth accused, who initially managed to escape, was arrested later.

The probe revealed that all four accused were drug users and allegedly committed the robberies to raise money to buy narcotics. The money extorted from drivers was reportedly transferred directly to the bank account of a suspected drug peddler.

Manoj, the prime accused, allegedly planned the robberies and identified potential targets. Preetham Prakash, a BCom graduate, was his associate, while Syed Shafi worked as a cab driver and Akhilesh was employed as a tattoo artist.
The gang initially used an autorickshaw to commit the robberies but later switched to a rented car to target drivers.
During interrogation, the accused allegedly confessed to committing around 30 robberies in three months. The police have so far traced and linked the gang to 11 incidents.
Investigators are also identifying other victims, as several drivers who lost relatively small amounts of money had not approached the police to file complaints.

fullParagraphs: Communist Party of India (CPI) general secretary D. Raja on Thursday (November 26, 2026) announced a three-day “Jail Bharo Andolan” from December 1 to 3 on a set of political and economic demands, including the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, implementation of women’s reservation, and a legal guarantee for Minimum Support Price (MSP) for farmers.

Addressing a press conference, Mr. Raja said the country was facing multiple crises, claiming that the economy was in a poor state, prices were rising and unemployment remained high. He also expressed concern over “increasing atrocities against minorities, Dalits, women and children.”

The CPI leader said Prime Minister Narendra Modi often spoke and wrote about the Constitution but he should be “truthful to the people and the country”. He said the Constitution made it clear that India should remain a secular democratic republic and noted that B.R. Ambedkar had rejected the idea of a theocratic state. Mr. Raja accused Mr. Modi of seeking to establish a “Hindu Rashtra”, which he described as a “unidimensional, monolithic neoliberal medieval social order” that perpetuated caste inequalities and subverted the Constitution.
Mr. Raja appealed to “all secular democratic forces” to unite against the BJP and work towards defeating the ruling party in the coming Assembly elections in five States.
He said the CPI had held informal discussions with the Samajwadi Party and the Congress regarding seat-sharing in Uttar Pradesh and Punjab.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The tariffs are not final yet, with the U.S. government opening a window for written comments and requests to testify by January 5, 2027. Public hearings will begin on January 25, 2027, following which the final action will be communicated.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.
“Strong bank and non-bank credit growth continues to support the domestic economy. Further, sustained double-digit export growth broadened the base of economic expansion,” they added.
Equity markets remained buoyant amid robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio investment inflows, while net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

fullParagraphs: Duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will be permitted until the end of March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) on Wednesday.

A notification issued on August 20 had allowed duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) scheme until December 31, 2026. Separately, the DGFT has allowed sugar mills time until September 30, 2027, to process the imported raw sugar and sell it in the domestic market.

The Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association Director General Deepak Ballani told The Hindu that price parity had prevailed over the past, making it viable for Indian importers to source raw sugar from international markets, primarily Brazil. Some imports have already begun.

The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season. It will also keep the prices stable, he said.

articles.title: Air passenger services see 35% inflation in Q2; banking, securities transaction witness deflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.
The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.
Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.
As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.
Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.
Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.
Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.
The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

The government in June came out with the maiden PPI data for both goods and services to better reflect price movement at producer's level, paving the way for phasing out wholesale price index (WPI)-based inflation numbers in the next five years. Thereafter, in August the services PPI data was issued.

articles.title: Global climate talks must shut door on fossil fuel ‘clout’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The failure of the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to agree on its central political statement, with countries unable to bridge their differences over fossil fuels and other key questions of climate action, has exposed the fragility of international climate cooperation. It should also sharpen scrutiny of who gets access to climate negotiations, whose interests they represent and what safeguards keep decisions accountable to the public.

The Türkiye summit ended without agreement on an overarching statement. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

The breakdown does not show that fossil fuel lobbying caused the impasse. But it does make more urgent a separate question about the credibility of the process. A forum that asks governments to make decisions in the global public interest must be transparent about who is seeking to shape those decisions, what interests they represent and how conflicts are managed.

The international climate negotiations that take place every year still lack a comprehensive, enforceable system to identify and manage conflicts of interest involving powerful commercial interests, including fossil fuel companies and state-owned energy businesses. The Antalya conference has underlined why that gap matters.

The fossil fuel industry’s record of muddying the waters is well documented. A 2017 study by Geoffrey Supran and Naomi Oreskes compared 187 ExxonMobil communications between 1977 and 2014, including internal documents, scientific publications and paid newspaper advertorials. It found that as the company’s communications became more public, they increasingly expressed doubt about climate science. The researchers concluded that ExxonMobil had contributed to climate science while promoting doubt about it in its advertorials.

An industry team discussed a 1998 draft of the Global Climate Science Communications Plan at the American Petroleum Institute’s headquarters. The plan’s stated goal was to persuade a majority of the American public that significant uncertainties remained in climate science and to raise questions among policymakers.

This history matters because companies with large investments in oil, gas and coal have a financial stake in how quickly those fuels are phased down, which technologies receive support and how the costs of the transition are distributed. That does not mean every company representative at a climate summit is there to obstruct progress, or that attendance proves influence over a decision. It, however, does mean commercial interests need to be visible and the process needs rules to prevent undue influence.

The scale of corporate participation in Antalya brings the issue into sharper focus. An analysis by a coalition of non-profits identified 103 major polluter groups with delegations at the summit, including fossil fuel businesses, financiers and companies from other high-emitting sectors. It also identified 30 banks whose fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025 amounted to more than $2.2 trillion.

These are the coalition’s classifications, not official UN figures. They do not establish that the companies or banks influenced the negotiations. But they show the scale of commercial interests present at a conference whose purpose is to limit global warming.

Lien Vandamme of the Center for International Environmental Law says the problem goes beyond the number of corporate participants. Although the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has introduced limited disclosure requirements, she argues that it still lacks a policy to curb corporate influence. “There is currently no policy to curb corporate influence within the UNFCCC process, and this is a fundamental problem,” she says. Once companies gain access, she argues, it becomes extremely difficult to monitor how they use it to influence negotiations.

The distinction between access and proven influence matters. The presence of a company representative does not show that a final decision was shaped by that company. But without public information about who participants represent, who funds their participation and what interests they promote and advance, it is difficult to assess where influence may be exercised.

The issue also extends beyond private companies. Some governments are major producers of oil and gas, while state-owned energy firms have direct commercial interests in the outcome of climate negotiations. Safeguards that examine only private corporations would leave a substantial part of the problem untouched.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthi-held capital hit after group targets Riyadh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Houthi media reported a series of Saudi airstrikes against territory held by the Iran-backed group including the capital Sanaa on Thursday (November 26, 2026), hours after it struck Riyadh.
The exchanges between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen have become near-daily in the country's revived civil war, which first began more than a decade ago.

The coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, said during the night that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital of Riyadh, where residents and an AFP journalist heard an explosion.
It also said it had destroyed a cruise missile launched towards the west of the country and a drone in the Jeddah region on the Red Sea.
"The air force of the Saudi enemy today launched a series of strikes at the capital Sanaa," the Houthis' press agency reported on Thursday morning.
An AFP journalist in Sanaa reported seeing smoke in the area of the airport. The Houthi news outlet Almasirah reported that the strikes targeted a factory and warehouses in Bani al-Harith.
Later on Thursday (November 26, 2026), residents of the key Houthi-controlled port of Hodeida told AFP they had heard jets flying over the city and loud explosions.
Almasirah said the strikes destroyed a wastewater treatment facility serving a densely populated district.
The Houthis said the day before they had struck two Saudi ports on the Red Sea, after Saudi strikes on Hodeida.
The coalition, meanwhile, said it had brought down a Houthi projectile targeting Jazan that had caused light damage and no civilian casualties.
Yemen's civil war burst back into life in July, bringing to an end a years-long truce that began in 2022.
The fighting has intensified since September, with the Houthis making significant territorial gains and bearing down on the temporary seat of the government in Aden.
